# Tool reference

<!-- Generated by scripts/dev/gen_docs.py from the tool registry. Do not edit. -->

pgharbor exposes **54 tools** in 9 groups. Every tool takes a
`connection` (a name from `pg_connections`); with a single configured connection it
may be left out. Tools adapt to the PostgreSQL version of the server (9.6 to 19).

Tools that write are listed only when some connection allows writing.

- [Core](#core) (8): `pg_connections`, `pg_request_access`, `pg_server_info`, `pg_query`, `pg_explain`, `pg_validate_sql`, `pg_policy`, `pg_audit_log`
- [Schema](#schema) (13): `pg_list_schemas`, `pg_list_tables`, `pg_describe_table`, `pg_list_objects`, `pg_describe_object`, `pg_get_ddl`, `pg_search`, `pg_search_source`, `pg_dependencies`, `pg_relationships`, `pg_schema_overview`, `pg_compare_schemas`, `pg_list_partitions`
- [Data](#data) (4): `pg_sample_rows`, `pg_count_rows`, `pg_column_stats`, `pg_export_query`
- [Performance](#performance) (12): `pg_activity`, `pg_locks`, `pg_top_queries`, `pg_table_stats`, `pg_index_stats`, `pg_bloat`, `pg_vacuum_status`, `pg_sizes`, `pg_cache_io`, `pg_progress`, `pg_database_stats`, `pg_stat_view`
- [Health](#health) (5): `pg_settings`, `pg_sequences_health`, `pg_wal_checkpoints`, `pg_index_advisor`, `pg_health_check`
- [Replication](#replication) (1): `pg_replication`
- [Security](#security) (4): `pg_roles`, `pg_privileges`, `pg_security_audit`, `pg_find_sensitive_columns`
- [Extensions](#extensions) (3): `pg_extensions`, `pg_extension_report`, `pg_integrity_check`
- [Administration](#administration) (4): `pg_execute`, `pg_maintenance`, `pg_signal_backend`, `pg_import_csv`

## Core

Connections, guarded queries and plans.

### `pg_connections`

List the configured PostgreSQL connections: name, environment, access mode, limits.

Start here. Every other tool takes a `connection` name from this list. No passwords
are ever shown. A connection marked `needs_approval` must be unlocked with
pg_request_access before use, and only when the user explicitly asked for that
environment.

### `pg_request_access`

Ask the user to approve the use of a protected connection (for example production).

Call this only when the user explicitly asked for that environment. The user sees a
dialog with the connection, the server and your `reason`. Never use a protected
connection as a fallback because another one failed.

`user_requested_this_environment` matters only for clients that cannot show dialogs:
set it to true only if the user named this environment in the conversation.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str` | required |
| `reason` | `str` | required |
| `user_requested_this_environment` | `bool` | `False` |

### `pg_server_info`

Show PostgreSQL version, uptime, current role and privileges, database size, key
settings, installed extensions and which optional features this server supports.

Use it first on an unfamiliar server: tools adapt to the version (9.6 to 19) and to
the extensions reported here.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |

### `pg_query`

Run one read-only SQL query (SELECT, WITH, VALUES, TABLE, SHOW) and return the rows.

The query is checked before it runs: one statement only, no writes, no functions with
side effects, protected tables and columns respected, and always inside a read-only
transaction with a time limit. Pass values through `params` ($1, $2, ...) instead of
concatenating them into the SQL.

Results are limited: `max_rows` (default from the connection, typically 200) and long
values are cut at `max_cell_chars`. When `has_more` is true, narrow the query or page
with `offset`. Prefer explicit column lists and a WHERE clause on large tables.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `sql` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `params` | `list[Any] \| None` | `None` |
| `max_rows` | `int \| None` | `None` |
| `offset` | `int` | `0` |
| `max_cell_chars` | `int \| None` | `None` |
| `format` | `"json"` \| `"markdown"` \| `"csv"` | `'json'` |

### `pg_explain`

Show the execution plan of a read query (EXPLAIN) without running it.

Returns the plan plus a summary: estimated cost and rows, tables touched and which of
them are read by sequential scan. Use it before running a heavy query and to
understand why a query is slow.

`analyze=true` really executes the query to measure it (EXPLAIN ANALYZE). It is only
available on connections configured with allow_explain_analyze.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `sql` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `params` | `list[Any] \| None` | `None` |
| `analyze` | `bool` | `False` |
| `verbose` | `bool` | `False` |
| `buffers` | `bool` | `False` |
| `settings` | `bool` | `False` |
| `format` | `"text"` \| `"json"` \| `"yaml"` \| `"xml"` | `'text'` |

### `pg_validate_sql`

Check a read query without executing it: syntax, object names, safety rules, result
columns with types, tables it would touch and its estimated cost.

Use it to test SQL you are about to give to the user, or to see exactly why pg_query
would refuse a statement.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `sql` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `params` | `list[Any] \| None` | `None` |

### `pg_policy`

Explain what is allowed on a connection: access mode, approval, limits, function
policy, protected tables and columns, denied relations.

Read it when a statement is refused, or before planning work on a connection you do
not know.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |

### `pg_audit_log`

Show the most recent entries of pgharbor's audit log: which tool ran, on which
connection, the SQL, the outcome and the rule that refused it.

Useful to review what was executed in this and previous sessions.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `limit` | `int` | `30` |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `outcome` | `'ok' \| 'refused' \| 'error' \| 'needs-approval' \| 'approved' \| 'bug' \| None` | `None` |

## Schema

Find your way around: objects, definitions, DDL, dependencies.

### `pg_list_schemas`

List the schemas (namespaces) of the database with owner, comment, how many tables,
views, sequences and functions each holds, and approximate size.

The first step when exploring a database. System schemas (pg_catalog,
information_schema) are left out unless `include_system` is true. Sizes come from the
planner statistics, so they are instant and slightly behind; pg_sizes measures.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `include_system` | `bool` | `False` |

### `pg_list_tables`

List tables (and optionally views, materialized views, foreign tables) with
estimated row count, size on disk and comment.

Filter by `schema` and by a name `pattern` (`*` and `?` wildcards; plain text matches
any name containing it). `order_by="size"` finds the biggest tables. Partitions are
hidden behind their parent unless `include_partitions` is true. Row counts are the
planner's estimates: instant, and close enough to choose a strategy.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `schema` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `pattern` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `kinds` | `list['table' \| 'view' \| 'materialized view' \| 'foreign table'] \| None` | `None` |
| `order_by` | `"name"` \| `"size"` \| `"rows"` | `'name'` |
| `include_partitions` | `bool` | `False` |
| `limit` | `int` | `100` |
| `offset` | `int` | `0` |

### `pg_describe_table`

Describe one table, view, materialized view or foreign table: columns with types,
defaults and comments; primary key, foreign keys (both directions), unique and check
constraints; indexes with size and usage; triggers; row security policies; partitions;
size, estimated rows and last vacuum/analyze.

`table` is `name` or `schema.name`. Read this before writing a query against a table.
`detail="summary"` returns only columns and keys.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `table` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `detail` | `"summary"` \| `"full"` | `'full'` |

### `pg_list_objects`

List objects of ONE kind: views, materialized views, sequences, functions,
procedures, aggregates, triggers, indexes, types, enums, domains, extensions, foreign
tables and servers, operators, casts, collations, languages, tablespaces, rules,
policies, statistics, publications, subscriptions, text search configs, access methods
or databases.

Each kind returns its own compact columns (a function: arguments, returns, language,
volatility; a sequence: type, last value, owning column; an index: table, method,
size). Filter by `schema` and by a name `pattern` (`*` and `?` wildcards; plain text
matches any name containing it). Kinds the server version does not have return an
empty list with a note. Tables are listed by pg_list_tables.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `kind` | `"view"` \| `"materialized_view"` \| `"sequence"` \| `"function"` \| `"procedure"` \| `"aggregate"` \| `"trigger"` \| `"event_trigger"` \| `"index"` \| `"type"` \| `"enum"` \| `"domain"` \| `"extension"` \| `"foreign_table"` \| `"foreign_server"` \| `"foreign_data_wrapper"` \| `"operator"` \| `"cast"` \| `"collation"` \| `"language"` \| `"tablespace"` \| `"rule"` \| `"policy"` \| `"statistics"` \| `"publication"` \| `"subscription"` \| `"text_search_config"` \| `"access_method"` \| `"database"` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `schema` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `pattern` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `limit` | `int` | `100` |
| `offset` | `int` | `0` |

### `pg_describe_object`

Describe one object that is not a table: a function, procedure, aggregate, sequence,
type, index, trigger, extension or schema.

Functions show every overload with arguments, return type, language, volatility,
security definer, parallel safety, cost, settings, comment and source code. Sequences
show type, range, last value, percent used and owning column. Types show enum labels,
domain base type and checks, composite attributes or range subtype. Extensions show
their version and the objects they created.

`name` is `name` or `schema.name`; a trigger can be `table.trigger`, and a function
accepts a signature such as `shop.order_total(bigint)`. `max_source_chars` cuts long
function bodies. For tables and views use pg_describe_table.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `str` | required |
| `kind` | `"function"` \| `"procedure"` \| `"aggregate"` \| `"sequence"` \| `"type"` \| `"index"` \| `"trigger"` \| `"extension"` \| `"schema"` \| `"table"` \| `"view"` \| `"materialized_view"` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `max_source_chars` | `int` | `3000` |

### `pg_get_ddl`

Rebuild the CREATE statement (DDL, as SQL text) of a table, view, materialized view,
function, procedure, sequence, type (enum, domain, composite, range), index, trigger or
schema.

A table comes with its columns (types, defaults, identity and generated columns, NOT
NULL), constraints, PARTITION BY / PARTITION OF, INHERITS, indexes, comments, triggers,
row level security and policies. Names are always schema-qualified. Owners and GRANTs
are not included. `name` is `name` or `schema.name`; a function accepts a signature such
as `shop.order_total(bigint)`. Use it to copy a structure or to review how an object was
defined.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `str` | required |
| `kind` | `"table"` \| `"view"` \| `"materialized_view"` \| `"function"` \| `"procedure"` \| `"sequence"` \| `"type"` \| `"index"` \| `"trigger"` \| `"schema"` | `'table'` |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |

### `pg_search`

Find database objects by name: tables, views, columns, functions, indexes,
sequences, types, enum labels, triggers, constraints, schemas, extensions, and text
inside comments.

Use it when you know a word (`invoice`, `customer_id`) but not where it lives. The
answer is grouped by kind, best matches first (exact name, then prefix, then
substring), each as `schema.object`. `query` matches anywhere in a name (`*` and `?`
are wildcards). `kinds` narrows the search, `schema` limits it to one schema, `limit`
is the maximum per kind. System schemas are skipped unless named.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `query` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `kinds` | `list['table' \| 'view' \| 'materialized_view' \| 'foreign_table' \| 'sequence' \| 'index' \| 'column' \| 'function' \| 'type' \| 'enum_label' \| 'trigger' \| 'constraint' \| 'schema' \| 'extension' \| 'comment'] \| None` | `None` |
| `schema` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `limit` | `int` | `50` |

### `pg_search_source`

Find functions, procedures, views, materialized views and triggers whose source code
contains a text, and return the matching lines with their line numbers.

Use it to answer "who uses this table or column?" in code that lives inside the
database, or "where is this function called?". `pattern` is plain text (case
insensitive); with `regex=true` it is a PostgreSQL regular expression. Line numbers
count from the first line of a function body or view definition. Code that belongs to
extensions is skipped. `limit` is the maximum number of objects.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `pattern` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `schema` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `kinds` | `list['function' \| 'procedure' \| 'view' \| 'materialized_view' \| 'trigger'] \| None` | `None` |
| `regex` | `bool` | `False` |
| `limit` | `int` | `30` |

### `pg_dependencies`

Show what depends on an object and what it depends on, to answer "what breaks if I
drop or change this?".

`dependents` are the views, materialized views, foreign keys from other tables,
functions that take the table's row type, sequences, indexes, triggers and column
defaults that use the object, followed through views of views up to `max_depth`.
`dependencies` are the tables, sequences, functions, types and extensions the object
needs. Each row says whether dropping the object needs CASCADE or removes it along with
the object. `name` is `name` or `schema.name`; a function needs its signature when it
has overloads.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `str` | required |
| `kind` | `"table"` \| `"view"` \| `"materialized_view"` \| `"sequence"` \| `"index"` \| `"function"` \| `"type"` | `'table'` |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `direction` | `"both"` \| `"dependents"` \| `"dependencies"` | `'both'` |
| `max_depth` | `int` | `3` |

### `pg_relationships`

Show the foreign key graph: which table references which, through which columns,
with ON DELETE / ON UPDATE actions.

`table` limits it to the relationships that touch one table (both directions);
`schema` to those that touch a schema; with neither it covers every user schema.
`format="mermaid"` returns a Mermaid `erDiagram` (entities with their key columns and
the relationships) that can be pasted into documentation or a Markdown viewer.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `schema` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `table` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `format` | `"json"` \| `"mermaid"` | `'json'` |
| `limit` | `int` | `200` |

### `pg_schema_overview`

Give a compact map of one schema that costs few tokens: one line per table in the
form `orders(id bigint PK, customer_id int FK->customers.id, status order_status)`
with primary keys, foreign key targets, unique columns and the estimated row count,
then the views (with their columns) and the number of functions, procedures and
sequences.

Use it first when you need to write queries against a schema. Partitions are folded
into their parent. `limit` caps the number of tables. For one table in full detail use
pg_describe_table.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `schema` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `limit` | `int` | `100` |

### `pg_compare_schemas`

Compare one schema on two connections (for example development and production, or
before and after a migration): what exists only in the source, only in the target, and
what differs.

Compared: tables, columns (type, nullability, default, identity), indexes, constraints,
views (definition), functions (signature, language, volatility and a hash of the body),
sequences and types.

`schema` is the schema on the source; `target_schema` the schema on the target when it
has another name. `include` limits the comparison to some of the kinds. Both
connections are read only, and both follow their approval rules. Nothing is changed.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `source_connection` | `str` | required |
| `target_connection` | `str` | required |
| `schema` | `str` | required |
| `target_schema` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `include` | `list['tables' \| 'columns' \| 'indexes' \| 'constraints' \| 'views' \| 'functions' \| 'sequences' \| 'types'] \| None` | `None` |

### `pg_list_partitions`

Show the partitions of a partitioned table as a tree: each partition with its bounds
(FOR VALUES ..., DEFAULT), its own partition key when it is partitioned again, estimated
rows and size on disk, plus the partitioning strategy (range, list, hash) and key.

On PostgreSQL 9.6, which has no declarative partitioning, it shows the table inheritance
children and their CHECK constraints instead. A table without partitions or children
answers with an empty list.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `table` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |

## Data

Look at rows and column statistics, through the guarded path.

### `pg_sample_rows`

Show a few rows of a table or view to see what the data looks like.

Pick `columns` to keep the answer small; by default every column the connection allows
is listed (columns protected by the connection's rules are left out, and values of
credential-like columns are redacted). `limit` is at most 100. By default the rows are
simply the first ones the server finds, in no particular order; `random=true` draws a
random sample instead (on a big table this reads the whole table once, so it can take a
while; the time limit of the connection applies). For a filtered read use pg_query.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `table` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `columns` | `list[str] \| None` | `None` |
| `limit` | `int` | `10` |
| `random` | `bool` | `False` |

### `pg_count_rows`

Count the rows of a table: an instant estimate from the planner statistics, and with
`exact=true` the real count(*).

The estimate costs nothing and is usually within a few percent; it adds up the
partitions or child tables of a partitioned table, and says when the table was last
analyzed (a table never analyzed has no useful estimate). The exact count reads the
whole table, so on a big table prefer the estimate, or filter with pg_query.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `table` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `exact` | `bool` | `False` |

### `pg_column_stats`

Describe the data of each column from the planner statistics, without reading the
table: fraction of NULLs, estimated number of distinct values, average width in bytes,
the most common values with their frequency (up to 10), the range of the histogram,
and the correlation with the physical order (near 1 or -1 means sorted).

Use it to see which columns are selective, skewed or mostly empty before writing a
query or an index. The numbers come from the last ANALYZE; a table never analyzed
has none, and the answer says so. For protected columns and columns whose name looks
like a credential only the statistics are given, never sample values.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `table` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `columns` | `list[str] \| None` | `None` |

### `pg_export_query`

Run a read-only query and save the result to a local file (CSV, JSON or JSON Lines)
instead of sending the rows to the conversation. Use it for results too big to read:
the answer holds only the path, the row count and the size.

The query goes through the same safety checks as pg_query (one statement, read only,
protected columns refused, credential-like columns redacted); use `params` ($1, $2, ...)
for values. `filename` is a plain file name, written to the connection's export folder
(default ~/pgharbor-exports). Up to `max_rows` rows, never more than 100,000; the file is
not overwritten unless `overwrite=true`. Exports can be turned off per connection.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `sql` | `str` | required |
| `filename` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `params` | `list[Any] \| None` | `None` |
| `format` | `"csv"` \| `"json"` \| `"jsonl"` | `'csv'` |
| `max_rows` | `int` | `10000` |
| `overwrite` | `bool` | `False` |

## Performance

What the server is doing and where time and space go.

### `pg_activity`

Show who is connected right now: sessions from pg_stat_activity with user, database,
application, client, state, wait event, how long the transaction, query and state have
lasted, the query text, which sessions block them (`blocked_by`), plus a summary by state
and the use of max_connections.

Use it to find long-running queries, sessions stuck "idle in transaction" and blocked
sessions. Idle sessions are hidden unless `include_idle` is true or `state="idle"` is
given. `min_duration_seconds` keeps sessions whose transaction or current state is at
least that old. Your own session is never listed. For the lock tree use pg_locks.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `state` | `'active' \| 'idle' \| 'idle in transaction' \| 'idle in transaction (aborted)' \| 'fastpath function call' \| 'disabled' \| None` | `None` |
| `min_duration_seconds` | `float \| None` | `None` |
| `include_idle` | `bool` | `False` |
| `database` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `limit` | `int` | `50` |

### `pg_locks`

Show lock waits as a blocking tree: which sessions wait, for how long and for which
lock or table, who holds it (pid, state, query, how long its transaction has been open),
the root blockers with how many sessions each one blocks, the strong
(ACCESS EXCLUSIVE) locks currently granted on user tables, and a count of locks by mode.

Use it when queries hang or `pg_activity` shows `blocked_by`. The wait time is counted
from the start of the waiting statement, so it is an upper bound. With
`only_blocked=false` it also lists the table locks every session holds or wants.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `only_blocked` | `bool` | `True` |
| `limit` | `int` | `50` |

### `pg_top_queries`

Rank the queries of the current database from pg_stat_statements: calls, total and
mean time, rows, share of the total time, blocks read and hit, temporary file volume,
WAL generated and planning time (WAL and planning on PostgreSQL 13+).

Use it to find what is slow or expensive. `order_by` is one of total_time, mean_time,
calls, rows, shared_blks_read, temp_blks_written or wal_bytes. `min_calls` ignores
statements that ran fewer times. Needs the pg_stat_statements extension. The query text is
normalized (constants replaced by $n) and cut; pass it to pg_explain to see the plan.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `order_by` | `"total_time"` \| `"mean_time"` \| `"calls"` \| `"rows"` \| `"shared_blks_read"` \| `"temp_blks_written"` \| `"wal_bytes"` | `'total_time'` |
| `limit` | `int` | `20` |
| `min_calls` | `int` | `1` |

### `pg_table_stats`

Show per-table activity from pg_stat_user_tables: sequential and index scans, rows
inserted, updated (and HOT updated) and deleted, live and dead rows, rows changed since
the last analyze, last vacuum/autovacuum/analyze/autoanalyze and the cache hit ratio.

Use it to find tables read by sequential scans, tables full of dead rows and tables
that autovacuum has not touched. Filter with `schema` and `table` (name, `schema.name`,
or a pattern with `*`). `order_by` picks the ranking; `cache_hit` lists the worst first.
Counters accumulate since the statistics were reset (shown as `counters_since`).

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `schema` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `table` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `order_by` | `"seq_scan"` \| `"seq_tup_read"` \| `"idx_scan"` \| `"live_tuples"` \| `"dead_tuples"` \| `"dead_percent"` \| `"modified_since_analyze"` \| `"inserts"` \| `"updates"` \| `"deletes"` \| `"cache_hit"` \| `"size"` | `'seq_scan'` |
| `limit` | `int` | `50` |

### `pg_index_stats`

List indexes with size, scans, tuples read and fetched, unique/primary/valid flags,
access method and definition, and find the ones to drop: `show="unused"` (never scanned
and not backing a constraint), `"duplicate"` (same columns, operator classes and
predicate as another index), `"redundant"` (columns are the leading columns of a longer
index) or `"invalid"` (a failed CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY).

Filter with `schema` and `table` (name, `schema.name` or a pattern with `*`). "Unused"
counts scans since the statistics reset (`counters_since`) on this server only: an index
used just on a replica or by a rare job looks unused here, so check before dropping.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `schema` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `table` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `show` | `"all"` \| `"unused"` \| `"duplicate"` \| `"redundant"` \| `"invalid"` | `'all'` |
| `limit` | `int` | `50` |

### `pg_bloat`

Estimate how much space tables and btree indexes waste (bloat) and rank them by
wasted bytes, without scanning anything: the estimate comes from the row counts and
average row widths in the planner statistics and is usually within 10 to 20 percent.

`kind` is tables, indexes or both; `schema` narrows the search; `min_wasted_bytes` hides
small waste. Relations never analyzed are skipped (run ANALYZE). For a measurement
instead of an estimate pass `exact_table` (`name` or `schema.name`): it reads that table
with the pgstattuple extension (pgstattuple_approx when available) and also reports the
density of its btree indexes, at the cost of reading the relation.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `schema` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `kind` | `"tables"` \| `"indexes"` \| `"both"` | `'both'` |
| `min_wasted_bytes` | `int` | `0` |
| `limit` | `int` | `30` |
| `exact_table` | `str \| None` | `None` |

### `pg_vacuum_status`

Report the state of vacuum and autovacuum: its configuration, the tables with the
most dead rows measured against their autovacuum threshold (honouring per-table
reloptions), transaction id and multixact age per table and per database as a percentage
of the wraparound limit, what holds back the oldest xmin (sessions, prepared
transactions, replication slots), vacuums running now with their progress, and the
autovacuum workers.

Use it when tables bloat, autovacuum seems idle, or before a wraparound emergency.
`limit` caps each list. For the per-table ranking by activity use pg_table_stats.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `limit` | `int` | `30` |

### `pg_sizes`

Find what takes the space: the biggest databases, schemas, tables (with heap data,
indexes and TOAST shown separately), indexes or tablespaces, largest first.

`scope` selects the kind of object. `schema` narrows tables and indexes to one schema.
Partitions are listed as tables of their own. Sizes include all forks of each relation;
use pg_bloat to see how much of a table is wasted.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `scope` | `"databases"` \| `"schemas"` \| `"tables"` \| `"indexes"` \| `"tablespaces"` | `'tables'` |
| `schema` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `limit` | `int` | `30` |

### `pg_cache_io`

Report cache effectiveness and I/O: the buffer cache hit ratio of the database, of
the tables and of the indexes (worst first among the busy ones), a summary of
pg_stat_io (PostgreSQL 16+), temporary file use, I/O timings when track_io_timing is
on, and, if the pg_buffercache extension is installed, the relations that occupy
shared_buffers.

A low hit ratio means reads go to the operating system or the disk; it does not count
the OS page cache, so a lower value is not always slow. `limit` caps each list.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `limit` | `int` | `20` |

### `pg_progress`

Show long operations that are running now with their progress: VACUUM, ANALYZE,
CLUSTER/VACUUM FULL, CREATE INDEX / REINDEX, base backups, COPY and REPACK, from the
pg_stat_progress_* views that exist on this server version.

Each operation lists the process, user, table, phase, how long it has run, percent done
when it can be computed and the raw counters. When nothing is running it says so. Use
it to answer "is it stuck or just slow?" for index builds and vacuums.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |

### `pg_database_stats`

Show pg_stat_database for the current database (or every database with
`all_databases=true`): connections, commits and rollbacks with the rollback ratio,
blocks read and hit with the cache hit ratio, rows returned, fetched, inserted, updated
and deleted, recovery conflicts, temporary files, deadlocks, I/O times, checksum
failures (PostgreSQL 12+), session counts and times (14+) and when the statistics were
last reset.

Counters accumulate since the reset. Use it for a first look at how a database is used
and to spot deadlocks, temp-file spills and a high rollback ratio.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `all_databases` | `bool` | `False` |

### `pg_stat_view`

Read any system view or catalog table from pg_catalog or information_schema by name,
for example pg_stat_user_functions, pg_stat_slru, pg_stat_ssl, pg_prepared_xacts,
pg_stat_wal, pg_stat_replication or pg_replication_slots.

Use it for everything that has no dedicated tool, and for views added by newer
PostgreSQL versions. `view` is `name` or `schema.name`; `columns` selects columns (all by
default); `order_by` sorts by a column, largest first unless `descending=false`. Names
are checked against the real columns on this server. Catalogs that hold credentials
(pg_authid, pg_shadow, pg_user_mapping...) are refused.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `view` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `columns` | `list[str] \| None` | `None` |
| `order_by` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `descending` | `bool` | `True` |
| `limit` | `int` | `50` |

## Health

Check-ups, index advice, settings, sequences, WAL.

### `pg_settings`

Search server configuration parameters (GUCs): current value with unit, default,
where the value comes from (default, configuration file with line, ALTER SYSTEM, ...),
whether changing it needs a restart, whether a restart is pending, and a short
description. Also lists errors found in the configuration files and the per-database and
per-role overrides (ALTER DATABASE/ROLE ... SET).

`pattern` matches parameter names (and descriptions), with `*` wildcards; `category`
filters by group (for example "Write-Ahead Log"); `changed_only` hides parameters still at
their default; `pending_restart_only` shows what waits for a restart.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `pattern` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `category` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `changed_only` | `bool` | `False` |
| `pending_restart_only` | `bool` | `False` |
| `limit` | `int` | `100` |

### `pg_sequences_health`

Find sequences that are running out of numbers: how much of the usable range each one
has consumed, how many values are left, and whether the column it feeds (serial or
identity) is a smaller integer type than the sequence, which makes the column overflow
first.

Only sequences at or above `threshold_percent` of their range are listed (default 50).
Sequences that cycle wrap around instead of failing and are flagged. A smallint or
integer key that is close to its limit needs an ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE bigint long
before the sequence ends.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `threshold_percent` | `int` | `50` |
| `limit` | `int` | `50` |

### `pg_wal_checkpoints`

Explain how checkpoints and WAL behave: scheduled versus forced checkpoints and the
buffers they wrote (pg_stat_bgwriter up to PostgreSQL 16, pg_stat_checkpointer from 17),
WAL volume (pg_stat_wal, 14+), the archiver (pg_stat_archiver), the current WAL position
and the WAL-related settings, ending with a one-line reading such as "forced
checkpoints: raise max_wal_size".

Use it for write-heavy servers, I/O spikes every few minutes and archiving problems.
Counters accumulate since the statistics reset.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |

### `pg_index_advisor`

Suggest indexes. Without `sql` it lists foreign keys with no supporting index (which
make deletes and joins on the parent scan the child table) and large tables read almost
only by sequential scans, each with a ready CREATE INDEX suggestion where one is clear.
With `sql` and `hypothetical_indexes` (a list of CREATE INDEX commands) it compares the
planner's estimated cost of the query before and after the indexes, without creating
anything: it needs the hypopg extension.

`table` (name, `schema.name` or pattern) narrows the heuristics. The query is checked by
the same rules as pg_query and is never executed, only planned. Indexes speed up reads and
slow down writes: add only the ones a real query needs.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `sql` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `table` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `hypothetical_indexes` | `list[str] \| None` | `None` |
| `limit` | `int` | `20` |

### `pg_health_check`

Run a quick DBA check-up and return findings ranked by severity: connection use, long
transactions, sessions idle in transaction, blocked sessions, transaction id wraparound,
dead rows, invalid and duplicate indexes, sequences near their end, cache hit ratio,
forced checkpoints, inactive replication slots, tables never analyzed or without a primary
key, deadlocks, temporary files, rollback ratio, settings waiting for a restart,
autovacuum, fsync/full_page_writes and orphaned prepared transactions.

Start here when asked "is this database healthy?". Every finding has a severity
(critical, warning, info, ok), the measured value, the threshold used and the tool that
goes deeper. A check that cannot run on this server version or with this role is reported
as `not_available` and the others still run. It only reads statistics and catalogs.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |

## Replication

Standbys, slots, publications and subscriptions.

### `pg_replication`

Show the replication state of the server in one answer: whether it is a primary or
a standby, connected standbys with lag, replication slots and the WAL they retain,
the WAL receiver and replay delay on a standby, publications with their tables,
subscriptions with their statistics, recovery conflicts and the settings that govern
replication.

Use it to check that replicas are healthy, to find an abandoned slot that makes the
disk fill with WAL, or to see what logical replication publishes. Connection strings
and passwords are never shown. A server without any replication says so plainly.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |

## Security

Roles, privileges, audits. Never returns a secret.

### `pg_roles`

List database roles (users and groups) with their attributes (superuser, createdb,
createrole, login, replication, bypassrls), connection limit, password expiry, the
roles each one belongs to (`member_of`) and its members, plus per-role settings.

Use it to see who can log in and who holds powerful attributes. Superusers also get
the password method of each login role (scram-sha-256, md5 or none); the hash itself is
never returned. `pattern` filters by name (`*` wildcard). Built-in `pg_*` roles are
hidden unless `include_system` is true. From PostgreSQL 16 memberships show their
admin/inherit/set options.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `pattern` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `include_system` | `bool` | `False` |
| `limit` | `int` | `100` |

### `pg_privileges`

Show access rights, in one of two ways. With `object`: who can do what on that
table (and its columns), schema, function, sequence or database, owner and PUBLIC
included. With `role`: everything that role may do (granted directly, through roles it
inherits, or to PUBLIC), the objects it owns and its default privileges.

`kind` says what `object` names (default table, views included); a function can be
`schema.name` or `name(argument types)` when overloaded. Pass `role="public"` to see
what every role can do. Pass one of `object` and `role`, not both. A superuser
bypasses all of these checks; the answer says so.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `object` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `role` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `kind` | `"table"` \| `"schema"` \| `"function"` \| `"sequence"` \| `"database"` | `'table'` |
| `limit` | `int` | `200` |

### `pg_security_audit`

Audit the database for security weaknesses and rank the findings as critical,
warning or info, each with a recommendation.

It checks superusers and powerful role attributes (CREATEROLE, REPLICATION, BYPASSRLS),
md5 password hashes, PUBLIC privileges and a PUBLIC-writable schema, SECURITY DEFINER
functions without a fixed search_path, row level security gaps, pg_hba rules with trust or
cleartext passwords, ssl, untrusted languages, risky extensions, file and program access
roles, foreign servers and event triggers. Each check runs on its own: one that the
server or the role cannot do becomes a note and the rest still run. Nothing is changed
and no secret is read.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |

### `pg_find_sensitive_columns`

Find columns that look like they hold sensitive data, judging by column name, comment
and type only: passwords, tokens and keys, CPF/CNPJ/SSN, emails, phones, payment cards,
birth dates, salaries, addresses and similar, in English and Portuguese.

For each match it gives the table, column, type, category, why it was flagged, whether
the table has row level security (`rls`) and whether it uses column-level grants
(`column_grants`). The data itself is never read. Use it to plan masking and access
control, or before exposing a schema to an application. `schema` narrows the search.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `schema` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `limit` | `int` | `100` |

## Extensions

Installed extensions and what they add; integrity checks.

### `pg_extensions`

List the extensions installed in this database (version, schema, whether a newer
version can be installed with ALTER EXTENSION ... UPDATE, comment) and the ones the
server could install with CREATE EXTENSION.

Use it to see what a database can do (pg_stat_statements, PostGIS, pgvector, pg_cron...)
and what is missing. `pattern` filters by name (`*` wildcard); `only_installed` skips the
available list. For the available ones it says whether installing needs a superuser
(trusted extensions, PostgreSQL 13+, only need CREATE on the database). pg_extension_report
describes one installed extension.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `pattern` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `only_installed` | `bool` | `False` |

### `pg_extension_report`

Report on one installed extension: version, schema, the objects it created
(functions, types, tables, operators), its settings, and extension-specific facts.

Specific parts exist for pg_stat_statements (entries), pg_buffercache (cache summary),
pg_trgm (trigram indexes), hypopg (hypothetical indexes), vector/pgvector (vector columns,
hnsw and ivfflat indexes), postgis (version, geometry columns, SRID, spatial indexes),
pg_cron (jobs and last runs), pg_partman (configured tables), pgaudit, postgres_fdw and
dblink (servers, foreign tables, never user mapping options), pgstattuple, pgcrypto and
timescaledb (hypertables). Any other extension gets the generic part. If the extension is
not installed the error says how to install it; pg_extensions lists what exists.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `extension` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |

### `pg_integrity_check`

Look for data integrity problems: invalid indexes, constraints added NOT VALID,
tables without a primary key, forgotten prepared transactions, disabled triggers
(including foreign key enforcement), collation versions that changed under the
server, data checksums off or failing, and sequences that no column owns.

`schema` limits the object checks to one schema. With `index` (the name of a b-tree
index) and the amcheck extension (PostgreSQL 10+) it also verifies that index's
structure with bt_index_check, which needs a superuser and reads the whole index. Nothing
is changed; each problem comes with a fix to apply yourself.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `connection` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `schema` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `index` | `str \| None` | `None` |

## Administration

Change the database. Only on connections configured for it, always confirmed by the user.

### `pg_execute`

*writes; needs access `read-write`*

Run ONE statement that changes data or structure: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, MERGE,
CALL (connections with access "read-write") or DDL and maintenance such as CREATE,
ALTER, DROP, GRANT, VACUUM (access "admin").

The user is asked to confirm before anything is committed. Start with `dry_run=true`:
the statement really runs inside a transaction that is then rolled back, so you can
show the user how many rows would change. Bind values with `params` ($1, $2, ...).

Not available on read-only connections: there, show the SQL to the user as text and
say that it was not executed. `confirmed_by_user` only matters for clients that cannot
show a confirmation dialog; set it to true only after the user clearly said yes to
this exact statement.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `sql` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str` | required |
| `params` | `list[Any] \| None` | `None` |
| `dry_run` | `bool` | `False` |
| `confirmed_by_user` | `bool` | `False` |

### `pg_maintenance`

*writes; needs access `admin`*

Run a maintenance command on a table, index or materialized view: ANALYZE, VACUUM
(plain, ANALYZE, FULL, FREEZE), REINDEX, REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW, or reset the
statistics counters.

`target` is `schema.name`; ANALYZE and VACUUM accept no target to cover the whole
database. `concurrently` applies to REINDEX (PostgreSQL 12+) and REFRESH, and avoids
blocking readers. VACUUM FULL and a plain REINDEX lock the table: warn the user.
Needs a connection with access "admin"; the user confirms every run.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `action` | `"analyze"` \| `"vacuum"` \| `"vacuum_analyze"` \| `"vacuum_full"` \| `"vacuum_freeze"` \| `"reindex_table"` \| `"reindex_index"` \| `"refresh_materialized_view"` \| `"reset_statistics"` | required |
| `connection` | `str` | required |
| `target` | `str \| None` | `None` |
| `concurrently` | `bool` | `False` |
| `timeout_seconds` | `int \| None` | `None` |
| `confirmed_by_user` | `bool` | `False` |

### `pg_signal_backend`

*writes; needs access `admin`*

Cancel the running query of another session (`cancel`) or close the session
entirely (`terminate`), by process id.

Find the pid with pg_activity or pg_locks. Prefer `cancel`: it stops the statement and
leaves the connection alive. `terminate` rolls back that session's transaction and
disconnects it. Needs a connection with access "admin"; the user confirms.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `pid` | `int` | required |
| `connection` | `str` | required |
| `action` | `"cancel"` \| `"terminate"` | `'cancel'` |
| `confirmed_by_user` | `bool` | `False` |

### `pg_import_csv`

*writes; needs access `read-write`*

Bulk-load a local CSV file into an existing table with COPY, in one transaction.

`filename` is the name of a file inside the import directory of the connection
(`import_dir` in the configuration, `~/pgharbor-imports` by default): no other path
is readable. `columns` gives the order of the file's columns when it differs from the
table. `dry_run=true` loads the file, reports the row count and rolls back. Needs a
connection with access "read-write" or "admin"; the user confirms.

| Parameter | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `table` | `str` | required |
| `filename` | `str` | required |
| `connection` | `str` | required |
| `columns` | `list[str] \| None` | `None` |
| `header` | `bool` | `True` |
| `delimiter` | `str` | `','` |
| `null` | `str` | `''` |
| `dry_run` | `bool` | `False` |
| `confirmed_by_user` | `bool` | `False` |
